title: 无衣
author: 佚名（《诗经·秦风》）
authorEn: Anonymous (Book of Songs, Airs of Qin)
intro: “Who says you have no clothes? Share my robe!” Soldiers of the state of Qin sing as they sharpen their weapons for war. A rousing marching song about comradeship, still quoted whenever people stand together.
analysis: 这是秦国士兵出征前唱的战歌。开头就是一句反问：“岂曰无衣？”——谁说你没有衣服？我的战袍和你一起穿！接着说：国君要出兵了，修好我们的戈和矛，你的敌人就是我的敌人。三章层层推进：同袍、同泽（内衣）、同裳（下衣），衣服越分越细，感情越来越亲；从“同仇”到“偕作”（一起行动）再到“偕行”（一起上战场），行动越来越近。句子短，节奏快，像喊口号一样有力，读起来能感到士兵们互相鼓励、团结一心的豪气。今天“同袍”“同仇敌忾”这些说法都和这首诗有关，“同袍”至今还用来称呼一起奋斗的战友。
analysisEn: This is a war song sung by soldiers of the state of Qin before battle. It opens with a challenge: 岂曰无衣 — “Who says you have no clothes?” If you have none, we’ll share my robe. Then: the king is raising an army, so let’s mend our spears and halberds; your enemy is my enemy. Each verse goes one step further. The clothing gets more personal — the outer robe, then the undershirt, then the lower garment — as the bond between the men grows closer; the action moves from sharing a foe to getting up together to marching off together. The lines are short and punchy, like a chant, and you can almost hear men slapping each other’s shoulders. That spirit is why the poem lasted: 同袍 (“sharing a robe”) is still used in Chinese for comrades-in-arms, and 同仇敌忾, “sharing the same hatred of the enemy”, echoes its words. Qin was the tough frontier state that would eventually unify China, and this song shows the fighting spirit people associated with it.
background: The Book of Songs gathers 305 songs from about the 11th to the 6th century BC. This one is from the state of Qin (秦), on the western frontier in today’s Shaanxi and Gansu, which fought constantly with nomadic peoples and later unified China in 221 BC. The author is unknown.
pronunciation: 泽 zé（通“襗”，贴身的内衣）；裳 cháng（下衣，古代读 cháng，不读 shang）；戟 jǐ；偕 xié；行 xíng。“裳”机器朗读易错，已在“朗读用字”列替换同音字。
version: 采用通行《毛诗》文本，全诗三章，每章五句；网站每章排三行。

lines.py: qǐ yuē wú yī, yǔ zǐ tóng páo
lines.lit: How can you say you have no clothes? I will share my robe with you.
lines.en: Who says you have nothing to wear? My robe is yours too.

lines.py: wáng yú xīng shī, xiū wǒ gē máo
lines.lit: The king is raising an army; let us mend our dagger-axes and spears.
lines.en: The king calls up his army — let’s get our spears ready.

lines.lit: With you I share one enemy!

lines.py: qǐ yuē wú yī, yǔ zǐ tóng zé
lines.lit: How can you say you have no clothes? I will share my undershirt with you.
lines.en: Who says you have nothing to wear? My shirt is yours too.

lines.py: wáng yú xīng shī, xiū wǒ máo jǐ
lines.lit: The king is raising an army; let us mend our spears and halberds.
lines.en: The king calls up his army — let’s get our halberds ready.

lines.lit: With you I will rise up!

lines.py: qǐ yuē wú yī, yǔ zǐ tóng cháng
lines.lit: How can you say you have no clothes? I will share my lower garment with you.
lines.en: Who says you have nothing to wear? My clothes are yours too.

lines.py: wáng yú xīng shī, xiū wǒ jiǎ bīng
lines.lit: The king is raising an army; let us mend our armour and weapons.
lines.en: The king calls up his army — let’s get our armour ready.

words.note: 岂：难道；今天“岂有此理”还用。
古代对人的尊称，“孔子”“老子”的“子”。
今天“兴师动众”比喻动用很多人。
古代兵器；“化干戈为玉帛”的“戈”。
古代兵器，矛和戈合在一起。

words.en: lower garment, a kind of skirt
words.note: 古代“上衣下裳”；今天“衣裳”读 yīshang。

imagery.name: 衣
imagery.zh: 战士们把自己的衣服分给同伴，衣服从外到内，象征同生共死的情谊。
imagery.en: Soldiers share their clothes, from outer robe to undershirt — a bond of brothers who will live or die together.
